claims.text: A two-stage solution-annealing and aging treatment will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy.
A solution anneal near 1100°C will homogenize the target alloy's microstructure.
Aging near 750°C will induce controlled precipitation.
An aging duration of 4–8 hours is suitable for inducing the desired precipitation.
The target alloy can contain roughly 30–40 at% Ti, roughly 30–40 at% Ni, and at least three additional elements at smaller concentrations.
The solution-annealed target alloy initially has a homogeneous microstructure.
The relevant elevated-temperature operating range is 600–900°C, with testing around 750°C.
The treatment will form a refined and uniformly distributed population of coherent precipitates in the target alloy.
The target-alloy precipitates will be analogous to the gamma-prime phase of conventional nickel-based superalloys.
Aging induces nucleation and controlled growth of the coherent precipitates.
The fine precipitates impede dislocation motion under elevated-temperature load.
Precipitation strengthening will increase elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the solution-annealed control.
Precipitation strengthening will increase creep resistance relative to the solution-annealed control.
The intervention will produce more than a 10% increase in elevated-temperature yield strength.
Excessive treatment can cause deleterious phase formation or grain coarsening, so processing must remain within thermal-stability limits.
Aging near 750°C for several hours must be carefully controlled to obtain the desired microstructure.
The optimal aging temperature and duration may vary with the minor-element additions.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on phase stability and the starting microstructure.
Identically composed control and intervention batches can be compared by elevated-temperature tensile and creep testing and by electron-microscopy characterization of precipitates.

The hypothesis is falsified if the aged material fails to achieve a statistically significant improvement of about 10% or more in strength and creep resistance, or if it fails to form the proposed fine, uniform precipitate population.

contradictions.description: The stated example allows Ti and Ni concentrations as high as 40 at%, while the boundary requires compliance with the query's high-entropy-alloy definition of 5–35 at% for each constituent.
